title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Design = Solutions

Design is about finding solutions.
Unfortunately, designers often reinvent solutions to problems that have already been solved.
This happens because it is hard to know:

How things were done before.
Why things were done a certain way.
How to reuse existing solutions.

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
section: How Can We Codify Design Knowledge?
text:
How Can We Codify Design Knowledge?

An effective and flexible design is difficult to get “right” the first time.
Yet experienced designers do make good designs.
New designers are usually overwhelmed by all the design options available.
Experienced designers evidently know something inexperienced ones don’t — what is it?

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
section: How Experienced Designers Solve a Problem
text:
How Experienced Designers Solve a Problem

Expert designers usually do not solve every problem from first principles — they reuse solutions that have worked for them in the past.
When they find a good solution, they use it again and again.
Such experience is part of what makes them experts.
These experiences can be recorded as design patterns.

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Excerpt from Last Week

“Good artists borrow (from other artists), but great artists steal!” — Pablo Picasso
Compelling visual design takes practice and experience — a natural part of which is study and critique of others’ work.

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Novelists Use Patterns

Novelists and playwrights rarely design their plots from scratch.
They follow patterns like “Tragically Flawed Hero” (Macbeth, Hamlet, etc.) or “The Romantic Novel” (countless romance novels).

Game Players Use Patterns

Chess players, Go players, and basketball players all rely on “patterns.”
Examples given in the source: the 1-4 offense pick-and-roll (basketball), a star-point joseki (Go), and the Queen’s Gambit (chess).

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
The Design Methods Hierarchy
Design knowledge can be organised from abstract to concrete:

Design Philosophy (most abstract)
Design Principles
Design Patterns
Design Idioms, Specific Knowledge and Tips (most concrete)

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Design Patterns vs. Design Guidelines

Design guidelines can be either abstract or concrete.
Abstract guidelines usually do not suggest how to solve a problem.
Concrete guidelines are usually too tailored to a specific interface.
Guidelines assume absolute validity, while design patterns emphasize effectiveness in a particular context.
Guidelines are more useful for describing requirements; patterns are useful tools for translating requirements into specific software solutions.

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Patterns vs. Idioms

Not every design idea that uses the pattern syntax is a pattern.
If an idea is too specific (e.g. programming-language specific), it is not a pattern — such specific ideas are called idioms.
Patterns also cannot be too general.
It must be clear how the pattern should be applied in a context.

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Patterns vs. Lexicon/Vocabulary

If a technique appears so often in a domain that everyone knows and uses it in almost any situation, it is most likely not a pattern.
Example, in game design: Player, Stage, Enemy, Gun shots — these are vocabulary, not patterns.

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
What Are Design Patterns…

“Patterns communicate insights into design problems, capturing the essence of the problems and their solutions in a compact form. They describe the problem in depth, the rationale for the solution, and some of the trade-offs in applying the solution.” — The Design of Sites, Van Duyne et al. 2003
“Each pattern describes a problem which occurs over and over again in our environment, and then describes the core of the solution to that problem, in such a way that you can use this solution a million times over, without ever doing it the same way twice.” — A Pattern Language, Alexander et al. 1977
“A pattern is the abstraction from a concrete form which keeps recurring in specific non-arbitrary contexts.” — Riehle and Zullighoven, Understanding and Using Patterns in Software Development

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
section: Christopher Alexander: Pattern 115 — Courtyards Which Live
text:
Christopher Alexander: Pattern 115 — Courtyards Which Live

Courtyards built in modern buildings are often “dead” — intended as private open spaces, but ending up unused.
Three ways courtyards fail:

Too little ambiguity between indoors and outdoors.
Not enough doors into the courtyard.
Too enclosed.

Therefore: place every courtyard so there is a view out to a larger open space; add at least two or three doors opening into it along natural paths; and add a roofed veranda or porch continuous with both the inside and the courtyard, following the ARCADE, GALLERY SURROUND, and SIX-FOOT BALCONY patterns.
Source: A Pattern Language, Alexander et al., 1977.


Photograph of a plant-filled courtyard with tiled arcades and columns, illustrating Alexander’s Pattern 115 “Courtyards Which Live”

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
The Nature of Design Patterns

Not too general and not too specific.
Use a solution “a million times over, without ever doing it the same way twice.”
Design patterns are a shared language for “building and planning towns, neighborhoods, houses, gardens, & rooms.”
Example: a beer hall is part of a center for public life, and needs spaces for groups to be alone — the ALCOVES pattern.

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Pattern Format
A pattern is typically documented with:

Pattern Name
Context
Forces
Problem Statement
Solution
Solution Sketch
Other Patterns to Consider

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Example – Alcoves

Pattern Title: Alcoves
Context: Collaborative and common areas in buildings.
Forces: Open spaces are inviting, but people want a sense of enclosure for private discussions.
Problem Statement: Create a space that invites collaboration but also supports private discussion.

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Example – Alcoves: Solution
“Make small places at the edge of any common room, usually no more than 6 feet wide and 3 to 6 feet deep and possibly much smaller. These alcoves should be large enough for two people to sit, chat, or play and sometimes large enough to contain a desk or a table.”

Page excerpt showing the Alcove pattern’s solution text alongside a sketch of a puzzle-piece-shaped room with small alcove extensions labelled “alcoves”

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
section: Many Patterns Form a Pattern Language
text:
Many Patterns Form a Pattern Language

The patterns within a domain should be organised into a logical or naturally intuitive structure.
Each pattern should indicate its relationship to other patterns and to the pattern language as a whole.
A pattern language helps by:

Noticing and naming common problems in a field of interest.
Describing key characteristics of effective solutions for a stated goal.
Helping the designer move from problem to problem in a logical way.
Allowing for many different paths through the design process.

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Pattern Languages

Alexander emphasized the importance of pattern languages — more than just collections of patterns.
Languages are sets of patterns that fill out a design space and are chosen to complement each other.
Forces in each pattern may explain its relations with other patterns.

title: Junior Narrative Designer Case Study: Elden Ring
section: Critical Case Analysis: Ludonarrative Harmony in Elden Ring
text:
Critical Case Analysis: Ludonarrative Harmony in Elden Ring
Elden Ring tells its story mostly through the world and gameplay rather than through direct exposition. Players explore, fight bosses, and choose their own path, and this way of playing matches the story itself: the Lands Between is a dangerous and mysterious place, so exploring and learning fits the narrative.
The game presents a broken and ruined world. Kingdoms have fallen, powerful demigods have become corrupted, and the natural order has collapsed. The player takes on the role of a Tarnished, once exiled but now called back to try to restore the Elden Ring.
The gameplay reflects this story directly. The world is dangerous and unforgiving — enemies are strong, bosses are difficult, and death happens often. This difficulty is not random; it reinforces the idea that the world is damaged and unstable. The player must learn from mistakes, grow stronger, and slowly come to understand the world. This alignment between what the player does and what the story communicates is known as ludonarrative harmony.
For example, when a player fights a powerful demigod like Godrick or Radahn, the difficulty of the fight demonstrates how powerful these characters are within the story. Their strength in gameplay reflects their importance in the narrative, and the challenge makes the world feel real and serious.
However, moments of ludonarrative dissonance can also occur. Sometimes certain enemies or bosses feel difficult without a clear story explanation — a random strong enemy in a small area might feel more like a gameplay obstacle than part of the narrative world. When this happens, the player may feel frustrated rather than immersed, and the emotional connection to the story weakens as the focus shifts from meaning to mechanics.
Overall, Elden Ring mostly succeeds in creating harmony between gameplay and story. The open world, the danger, and the sense of mystery all support the narrative themes of decay, ambition, and struggle.

title: Junior Narrative Designer Case Study: Elden Ring
text:
Storytelling Techniques
Elden Ring uses both explicit and environmental storytelling, but it relies far more heavily on environmental methods.
Explicit storytelling is limited. There are some cutscenes, especially during boss introductions or major story moments, and NPCs speak to the player and provide hints about quests. However, the dialogue is often short and unclear, with characters speaking in mysterious or poetic ways rather than explaining events directly. This design choice makes the player work harder to understand the story, paying attention to small details instead of relying on long cinematic scenes.
Environmental storytelling is the strongest storytelling method in the game. The world itself tells the story. For example, exploring Stormveil Castle reveals broken walls, dead soldiers, and signs of battle, showing that the castle was once powerful but has now fallen into chaos. In Caelid, the sky, the diseased land, and strange creatures show the impact of Scarlet Rot without needing long explanations. Even item descriptions contribute to this method, teaching players about past events, characters, and wars through small details. This approach follows the principle of “show, don’t tell”: instead of explaining everything, the game allows players to experience the consequences of past events through the environment.
Player choice versus story is also carefully balanced. Elden Ring gives players a high level of freedom — they can explore areas in different orders, choose which bosses to fight first, and build their characters around strength, magic, faith, dexterity, or hybrid combinations. This freedom gives players a sense of control and personal journey. However, the main story outcomes remain authored by the developers; the player cannot completely change the world’s history, and the endings are pre-written options. This balance between freedom and structure allows players to feel independent while still following a meaningful story.

title: Junior Narrative Designer Case Study: Elden Ring
section: Creative Design Proposal: The Shattered Citadel
text:
Creative Design Proposal: The Shattered Citadel

World-Building

Setting: A floating citadel that only appears at night, where gravity changes and platforms float.
Rules: Gravity shifts in certain areas, platforms float in a set pattern, and magic behaves unpredictably.
History: The citadel once belonged to a sorcerer family. Torn banners, journals, and broken towers tell the story of its fall.
Conflict: The citadel’s unstable magic threatens the Lands Between, and the player must find a way to fix it.

The Shattered Citadel fits naturally within the world of Elden Ring because it builds on themes already present in the base game — ambition, decay, and consequence. By combining environmental storytelling, a strong character arc, and a mechanic directly tied to the area’s history, the DLC maintains internal consistency while introducing something new to the Lands Between.


Character and Motivation
Lyra, the last remaining guardian of the Shattered Citadel, once served the sorcerer dynasty that ruled it and believed strongly in their goal of controlling time. When their experiments failed and the citadel shattered, she survived but became trapped in the time loop they created, leaving her feeling responsible for what happened.
Visual design and silhouette: Lyra wears dark silver armour with deep blue details that glow faintly. Her most distinctive feature is an hourglass-shaped helmet, inside which faint golden sand slowly falls, symbolising the unstable time magic of the citadel. She carries a long curved blade infused with time energy, and her cape flickers slightly as she moves, as if not fully stable in the present moment. Her silhouette is tall and elegant but slightly fragmented, reflecting the broken state of the citadel — and the hourglass helmet makes her instantly recognisable from a distance, an important quality in character design.
Motivation: At the start of the DLC, Lyra does not trust the player, believing outsiders caused the citadel’s fall. She sees herself as its final protector and refuses to accept that the sorcerers were responsible for their own downfall. Her goal is to protect what remains of the citadel and keep its knowledge safe, though she is also weary of being trapped in an endless loop.
Character arc: As the player explores the citadel and uncovers the truth about the failed experiments, Lyra slowly realises that the sorcerers’ ambition caused the disaster, and she begins to question whether protecting the citadel is truly right. By the end of the DLC, she accepts that the citadel must either be stabilised in a new way or allowed to end. If the player chooses to break the time loop, Lyra finally becomes free from her duty. Her arc reflects a theme of acceptance — that trying to control time and preserve the past can cause more harm than good.


Mechanics and Narrative Link
New mechanic: Time-shift areas change depending on the player’s actions, with enemies and platforms moving differently in response.
Why it fits the story: This mechanic makes players feel that the citadel itself is unstable, matching the story’s themes of discovery and danger.

text:
Reflection
“Show, don’t tell” is often more effective in games than in films or books because games are interactive. In a film, the audience watches the story; in a game, the player experiences it. This difference matters. When a game shows something through gameplay or environment instead of explaining it directly, the player feels more connected to the story.
In Elden Ring, the world tells its story through ruins, enemies, item descriptions, and boss fights rather than long explanations. Exploring a destroyed castle or land affected by Scarlet Rot lets the player understand that something terrible happened without needing a cutscene. This creates mystery, encourages curiosity, and makes the player active in discovering meaning rather than passively receiving it.
This idea shaped the design of the Shattered Citadel DLC. Rather than explaining everything directly, the design focuses on environmental storytelling — broken hourglasses, unstable gravity, and magic cracks in the sky all show that time magic went wrong, letting the player learn history by exploring rather than being told.
The Hero’s Journey also influenced Lyra’s character design. In many hero stories, a mentor or guardian figure helps guide the protagonist, often resisting change at first. Lyra’s initial distrust of the player reflects the “refusal of the call” stage, and her development mirrors the idea that growth comes from facing reality instead of avoiding it.
Overall, this project highlighted that strong narrative design is not just about writing a good story — it is about connecting gameplay, world design, and character development so that everything supports the same theme. When mechanics and story work together, the experience feels deeper and more meaningful.

title: Junior Narrative Designer Case Study: Elden Ring
text:
Visuals
Two concept visuals were created to support the DLC: one for the environment and one for the main NPC. These visuals help communicate the story, themes, and gameplay ideas without relying on long text explanations, making it easier to see how the Shattered Citadel works and how Lyra connects to its story.
Shattered Citadel — Environment Concept: The Shattered Citadel is depicted as floating and broken, showing that time in this area is unstable. Towers and platforms are suspended in the air, creating a sense of danger and mystery. Glowing cracks and drifting golden sand represent the effects of failed time experiments by the sorcerers. The design also supports gameplay, since floating platforms can create puzzles and Time Shift challenges. The environment communicates a story of ambition, failure, and chaos without dialogue or cutscenes, helping the player understand the DLC’s theme simply by looking around.
Lyra, the Timebound Guardian — Character Concept: Lyra’s hourglass-shaped helmet clearly signals her connection to the time loop. Her glowing sword and partially broken cape reflect the unstable magic of the citadel, while the blue and silver colour palette visually links her to the environment. The design communicates that she is both a guardian and a prisoner of the broken time loop. Her distinct silhouette ensures players recognise her immediately, reinforcing her character arc and connecting her visually to the gameplay mechanics and the wider story.

text:
Summary
Elden Ring achieves much of its emotional power through ludonarrative harmony, using difficulty, exploration, and environmental detail to reinforce its themes of decay, ambition, and struggle, while occasional moments of dissonance show how easily that connection can break. Its heavy reliance on environmental storytelling over explicit exposition, combined with a careful balance between player freedom and authored story structure, offers a model for narrative design. Applying these same principles to the Shattered Citadel DLC — through world-building, a character arc built on acceptance, and a mechanic tied directly to the setting’s history — demonstrates how “show, don’t tell” can be carried from analysis into original creative practice, ultimately reinforcing that strong narrative design depends on gameplay, world, and character all supporting a single unified theme.

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Motivation
This section explores why designers need a shared vocabulary for recording and reusing good solutions.

A decorative vector graphic accompanying this section’s title slide; its exact appearance is not recoverable from the source material, but it marks the transition into the Motivation topic

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Design = Solutions

Design is about finding solutions.
Unfortunately, designers often reinvent solutions that already exist.
It is hard to know:

How things were done before
Why things were done a certain way
How to reuse solutions

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
section: How Can We Codify Design Knowledge?
text:
How Can We Codify Design Knowledge?

An effective and flexible design is difficult to get “right” the first time.
Yet experienced designers do make good designs.
New designers are usually overwhelmed by all the design options available.
Experienced designers evidently know something inexperienced ones don’t — what is it?

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
section: How Experienced Designers Solve a Problem
text:
How Experienced Designers Solve a Problem

Expert designers usually do not solve every problem from first principles — they reuse solutions that have worked for them in the past.
When they find a good solution, they use it again and again.
Such experience is part of what makes them experts.
Such experiences can be recorded as design patterns.

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Excerpt from Last Week

“Good artists borrow (from other artists), but great artists steal!” — Pablo Picasso


Compelling visual design takes practice and experience — a natural part of which is study and critique of others’ work.


Portrait of Pablo Picasso, whose remark on artists borrowing and stealing ideas frames the discussion of reusing design solutions

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Novelists Use Patterns

Novelists and playwrights rarely design their plots from scratch.
They follow patterns like “Tragically Flawed Hero” (Macbeth, Hamlet, etc.) or “The Romantic Novel” (countless romance novels).




Illustration associated with Hamlet, used here to represent the “Tragically Flawed Hero” narrative pattern found across many plays





A romance novel cover representing “The Romantic Novel” pattern that recurs across countless works in that genre

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Game Players Use Patterns

Chess players, Go players, and basketball players all rely on “patterns.”
Examples given:

The 1-4 offense pick-and-roll (basketball)
A star-point Joseki in Go
The Queen’s Gambit (chess opening)





Diagram of a basketball 1-4 offense pick-and-roll play, illustrating a recognized tactical pattern players reuse in games





A Go board diagram illustrating a star-point joseki, a well-known recurring opening pattern in the game of Go

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
The Design Methods Hierarchy
Design knowledge can be organized from abstract to concrete:

Design Philosophy — most abstract
Design Principles
Design Patterns
Design Idioms, Specific Knowledge and Tips — most concrete

An arrow running through the hierarchy shows the movement from abstract guidance toward concrete, actionable knowledge.

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Design Patterns vs. Design Guidelines

Design guidelines can be either abstract or concrete.
Abstract guidelines usually do not suggest how to solve a problem.
Concrete guidelines are usually too tailored to a specific interface.
Guidelines usually assume absolute validity, while design patterns emphasize effectiveness in a particular context.
Guidelines are more useful for describing requirements; patterns are useful tools for translating requirements into specific software solutions.

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Patterns vs. Idioms

Not every design idea that uses the pattern syntax is actually a pattern.
If an idea is too specific (e.g., programming-language specific), it is not a pattern — such specific ideas are called idioms.
Similarly, patterns cannot be too general.
It must be clear how the pattern should be applied in a context.

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Patterns vs. Lexicon/Vocabulary

If a technique appears so often in a domain that everyone knows and uses it in almost any situation, it is most likely not a pattern — it is vocabulary.
Example, in game design:

Player
Stage
Enemy
Gun shots

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
What Are Design Patterns…

“Patterns communicate insights into design problems, capturing the essence of the problems and their solutions in a compact form. They describe the problem in depth, the rationale for the solution, and some of the trade-offs in applying the solution.” — The Design of Sites, Van Duyne et al., 2003


“Each pattern describes a problem which occurs over and over again in our environment, and then describes the core of the solution to that problem, in such a way that you can use this solution a million times over, without ever doing it the same way twice.” — A Pattern Language, Alexander et al., 1977


“A pattern is the abstraction from a concrete form which keeps recurring in specific non-arbitrary contexts.” — “Understanding and Using Patterns in Software Development,” Dirk Riehle and Heinz Züllighoven

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Design Patterns: A Brief History
A (very) brief history…

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Christopher Alexander
Alexander wrote patterns for architecture across three books:

The Timeless Way of Building
A Pattern Language
The Oregon Experiment

His work is organized at multiple levels — towns, buildings, and construction — forming a network that together makes up a language.



Cover of “A Pattern Language: Towns, Buildings, Construction” by Christopher Alexander, Sara Ishikawa, and Murray Silverstein — the foundational text that introduced pattern languages for architecture





Cover of “The Timeless Way of Building” by Christopher Alexander, the companion volume explaining the philosophy behind A Pattern Language

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Christopher Alexander (cont.)
Pattern 115: COURTYARDS WHICH LIVE

The courtyards built in modern buildings are very often dead. They are intended as private open spaces for people to use, but end up unused, full of gravel and abstract sculptures.
Three ways such courtyards fail:

There is too little ambiguity between indoors and outdoors.
There are not enough doors into the courtyard.
They are too enclosed.


Therefore: Place every courtyard so there is a view out to some larger open space; place it so at least two or three doors open from the building into it, along the natural paths that cross the courtyard. At one edge, beside a door, build a roofed veranda or porch continuous with both the inside and the courtyard — following the patterns for ARCADE (119), GALLERY SURROUND (166), and SIX-FOOT BALCONY (167).
Source: ‘A Pattern Language,’ Alexander et al., 1977

Photograph of a sunlit courtyard with arched colonnades and potted palms, illustrating the kind of lively, well-connected courtyard the pattern describes

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
The Nature of Design Patterns

Not too general and not too specific.
Use a solution “a million times over, without ever doing it the same way twice.”
Design patterns are a shared language for “building and planning towns, neighborhoods, houses, gardens, & rooms.”
Example: A beer hall is part of a center for public life, yet it also needs spaces for groups to be alone — this need is met by the ALCOVES pattern.

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Pattern Format
A pattern is typically documented with the following elements:

Pattern Name
Context
Forces
Problem Statement
Solution
Solution Sketch
Other Patterns to Consider

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Example: Alcoves — Context & Problem
Pattern Title: Alcoves

Context: Collaborative and common areas in buildings.
Forces: Open spaces are inviting, but people want a sense of enclosure for private discussions.
Problem Statement: Create a space that invites collaboration but also supports private discussion.

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Example: Alcoves — Solution & Sketch
Solution: Make small places at the edge of any common room, usually no more than 6 feet wide and 3 to 6 feet deep, and possibly much smaller. These alcoves should be large enough for two people to sit, chat, or play, and sometimes large enough to contain a desk or a table.

A page reproducing the Alcoves pattern text alongside its accompanying sketch, showing small recessed seating areas branching off a central common room

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
section: Many Patterns Form a Pattern Language
text:
Many Patterns Form a Pattern Language

The patterns within a particular domain should be organized into a logical or naturally intuitive structure. Each pattern should indicate its relationship to other patterns and to the pattern language as a whole.
Such a language helps by:

Noticing and naming the common problems in a field of interest
Describing the key characteristics of effective solutions for meeting some stated goal
Helping the designer move from problem to problem in a logical way
Allowing for many different paths through the design process

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Pattern Languages

Alexander emphasized the importance of pattern languages — more than just collections of patterns.
Languages are sets of patterns that fill out a design space and are chosen to complement each other.
Forces described in each pattern may explain its relations with other patterns.

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
section: A Pattern Language for Interactive Exhibits
text:
A Pattern Language for Interactive Exhibits
From [Borchers 2001], patterns for interactive exhibits are organized hierarchically:

Interactive Exhibit branches into Attract Visitor, Engage Visitor, and Deliver Message.
These lead to sub-patterns such as Simple Impress., Innovative Appearance, Domain-Appropriate Dev., Universal Access, and Immediate Feedback.
Which further lead to more specific patterns: New Input Dev., Invisible Hardware, Adjustable Height, Incremental Revealing, and Closed Loop.
At the most concrete level: Sparse Layout, Script Font, Coarse-Motoric Input, Dynamic Descriptor, Flat & Narrow Tree, and Batons.


A tree diagram showing how the abstract goal of an “Interactive Exhibit” branches through mid-level patterns like Universal Access and Incremental Revealing down to concrete design patterns such as Batons and Sparse Layout, illustrating a full pattern language

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Discussion

What’s the difference between design patterns and some experts’ tips in design?
Why is context required in documenting a pattern?
Can design patterns replace hands-on practice in design?

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
From Architecture to Computer Science

In the early 1990s, Gamma et al. borrowed the idea of patterns from architecture and applied it to software engineering.
The goal was to communicate object-oriented software design problems and their solutions.


Cover of “Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software” by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson, and John Vlissides — the influential book (the “Gang of Four”) that brought Alexander’s pattern concept into software engineering

title: Design Patterns: UIs, Games, Learning
text:
Patterns in HCI/UI Design
The idea of patterns extended further into human-computer interaction and interface design, drawing on resources including:

Designing Interfaces: Patterns for Effective Interaction Design [Tidwell 2005]
The Design of Sites [Van Duyne et al. 2002]
A Pattern Approach to Interaction Design [Borchers 2001]
Online repositories: http://www.hcipatterns.org/ and http://www.visi.com/~snowfall/InteractionPatterns.html




Cover of “Designing Interfaces” by Jenifer Tidwell, featuring a mandarin duck, presenting patterns for effective interaction design





Cover of “A Pattern Approach to Interaction Design” by Jan Borchers, part of the Software Design Patterns series, applying pattern language ideas to interactive systems





Cover of “The Design of Sites” by Douglas van Duyne and colleagues, a book of patterns for effective web design referenced alongside Tidwell’s and Borchers’ work

text: Welcome to the first stage of your table-top board game development journey. Over the course of one week, you will design a simple, innovative table-top game that can be explained and played using minimal components. The challenge is to create a game with a compelling objective and straightforward rules, while focusing on creativity and player engagement within a two-player format. This lesson walks you through the objective, the deliverables you need to produce, the constraints you must design within, and a set of sample ideas and mechanics to inspire your own concept.

title: Stage 1: Game Concept and Design Brief
text:
Objective
This week, your task is to develop a simple, innovative table-top game that can be explained and played using minimal components. The game should offer a compelling objective and straightforward rules, focusing on creativity and player engagement within a two-player format. Keep the design lean: the strength of your concept should come from clever mechanics and clear rules, not from a large number of components.

title: Stage 1: Game Concept and Design Brief
text:
Deliverables
Your submission for this stage consists of three parts:

Game Concept and Rules Document. Your game’s concept and rules need to be concisely presented within a two-page limit.

Page 1: A short description and instructions for your game, clearly outlining the objective, basic rules, and any unique gameplay elements.
Page 2: The game board or main layout, designed to be engaging and functional for the gameplay.

Initial Design Sketches/Digital Representations. Provide sketches or digital representations of any additional game components such as cards, tokens, or objects that enhance the gameplay. These should be supplementary and not exceed the core game’s two-page presentation.
Blog Post Reflection. Craft a reflective blog post detailing the process of developing your game concept, focusing on creative challenges, design decisions, and the anticipated player experience.

title: Stage 1: Game Concept and Design Brief
text:
Constraints and Limitations
Work within the following boundaries as you design your game:

The entire game must fit on 2 x A4 pieces of paper.
You are encouraged to design or use additional components like cards and tokens, keeping in mind the game’s expansion in later stages.
The game should be designed for two players initially, with plans to adapt it for multiple players.
Any extra items needed to play the game, such as six-sided dice, should be commonly available or easily substitutable (e.g., pencils, coins, or markers). Websites such as https://www.random.org/dice can substitute physical dice if necessary.
Your game and any additional components can be drawn by hand or created digitally. Ensure any photos are clear and well-lit.

title: Stage 1: Game Concept and Design Brief
text:
Submission Format

Compile your game concept, rules, and board into a single Word or PDF document. Include photos or digital files of additional components if applicable.
Submit the reflective blog post as a separate document or via a blog link, detailing your creative process and concept development journey.

title: Stage 1: Game Concept and Design Brief
text:
Sample Ideas
To spark your thinking, here are ten sample game concepts, each showing how a title, board description, objective, player interactions, unique mechanism, and game elements can fit together into a coherent design.
Monster March — Board: a town with houses, a forest, and a safe zone. Objective: escape monsters to the safe zone. Player interactions: use tokens to move monsters. Unique mechanism: a spinner for movement and monster actions. Rules summary: spin and move, using tokens to direct monsters. Gameplay example: use a token to redirect a monster towards a rival. Game elements: spinner, monster tokens, “scare” tokens, player pieces.
Garden Grow — Board: garden plots with various plants. Objective: grow the most vibrant garden. Player interactions: plant weeds in others’ gardens. Unique mechanism: weather dice affecting growth. Rules summary: roll for actions, with weather dice influencing plant growth. Gameplay example: a rain result on the weather dice accelerates growth. Game elements: weather dice, plant tokens, weed tokens, player pieces.
Pirate Plunder — Board: a treasure map with paths, traps, and treasures. Objective: collect coins and complete the puzzle first. Player interactions: set traps to delay others. Unique mechanism: puzzle pieces at treasure spots. Rules summary: move to collect, use traps to slow down others, and complete the puzzle. Gameplay example: find a piece that adds to your treasure map puzzle. Game elements: treasure coins, puzzle pieces, traps, player pieces.
Space Jump — Board: a galaxy map with planets and black holes. Objective: be first to jump back to Earth. Player interactions: pull others into gravity wells. Unique mechanism: gravity dice for jumps or black holes. Rules summary: roll to jump between planets, with gravity dice determining hazards. Gameplay example: rolling a black hole makes a player skip a turn. Game elements: gravity dice, player spacecraft pieces.
Critter Race — Board: a backyard path with natural obstacles. Objective: race your critter to the finish line. Player interactions: place obstacles in opponents’ paths. Unique mechanism: critter dice for overcoming obstacles. Rules summary: roll critter dice to move and navigate obstacles. Gameplay example: rolling a “dig” bypasses a rock obstacle. Game elements: critter dice, obstacles (rocks, ponds), player critters.
Wizard’s Duel — Board: a circular duel arena with spell zones. Objective: reach the centre to win the duel. Player interactions: cast spells to hinder opponents. Unique mechanism: a spell wheel for casting power. Rules summary: spin to cast spells, aiming to push opponents back. Gameplay example: spinning a “freeze” stops an opponent’s advance. Game elements: spell wheel, spell tokens (freeze, push), player wizards.
Museum Heist — Board: a museum layout with exhibits and lasers. Objective: steal an artifact and escape first. Player interactions: activate alarms against rivals. Unique mechanism: a laser pointer for navigating lasers. Rules summary: move to steal, using the laser pointer to avoid security. Gameplay example: navigate a laser section without touching the beam. Game elements: laser pointer, artifact tokens, alarm tokens, player thieves.

Unique mechanism: dice to “draw” stars for constellations. Rules summary: roll to connect stars, with clouds blocking paths. Gameplay example: rolling to connect the last two stars of Orion’s Belt. Game elements: star dice, constellation guides, cloud markers, player astronomers.

title: Stage 1: Game Concept and Design Brief
text:
Common Game Mechanics
Understanding established game mechanics can help you build your own concept on solid foundations. The table below summarises some of the most frequently used mechanics in board games and a well-known example of each.







Game Mechanic
Description




Roll-and-Move
Players roll dice and move pieces based on the outcome, e.g., Monopoly.


Set Collection
Players collect certain sets of cards or tokens to achieve a goal, e.g., Ticket to Ride.


Deck Building
Players start with a basic deck of cards and acquire more powerful cards to improve their deck over time, e.g., Dominion.


Worker Placement
Players place tokens on specific spots on the board to take actions or gain resources, e.g., Agricola.


Area Control
Players compete to dominate specific areas or territories on the board, e.g., Risk.


Tile Placement
Players place tiles to create or expand game areas, often scoring points based on placement, e.g., Carcassonne.


Resource Management
Players collect and manage resources (e.g., wood, stone, gold) to build structures, units, or points, e.g., Catan.


Auction/Bidding
Players bid resources or points to gain advantages or items in the game, e.g., Power Grid.


Cooperative Play
Players work together towards a common goal, often against the game itself, e.g., Pandemic.


Card Drafting
Players select cards from a shared pool to gain some advantage or fulfil objectives, e.g., 7 Wonders.


Hidden Roles
Players have secret roles or objectives unknown to others, creating tension and bluffing opportunities, e.g., The Resistance.


Dice Rolling
Dice determine outcomes or resources, with players often trying to mitigate luck through strategy, e.g., King of Tokyo.


Simulation
The game simulates a real-life process, system, or situation, requiring strategic planning and resource allocation, e.g., Terraforming Mars.


Push Your Luck
Players take risks to potentially gain more rewards, knowing they might lose everything they’ve gained, e.g., Quacks of Quedlinburg.


Point-to-Point Movement
Players move pieces from one discrete point to another, often to strategically position themselves or block opponents, e.g., Tsuro.


Narrative/Storytelling
The game includes a strong narrative element, with players’ actions affecting the direction and outcome of the story, e.g., Betrayal at House on the Hill.


Pattern Building
Players arrange pieces or cards to create specific patterns or configurations for points or achievements, e.g., Azul.

title: Stage 1: Game Concept and Design Brief
text:
Worked Example: A Turn-by-Turn Flow
To see how these mechanics can combine into a working game loop, consider the following flow, based on a treasure-collecting game similar to Pirate Plunder. Each player starts at the dock and takes turns rolling dice, moving along a path, and reacting to what they find, until someone collects all the puzzle pieces and races back to the ship to win.



A flowchart of a turn-based treasure game: players start at the dock, roll dice, move along the path, and either find a treasure spot (collecting a coin and puzzle piece, then setting a trap for others) or encounter a trap (being taken back or continuing on); each turn ends by checking whether all puzzle pieces have been collected, looping back to rolling dice until a player reaches the ship with the complete puzzle to win.


This kind of diagram is a useful design tool in its own right: mapping out your own game’s turn structure as a flowchart can help you spot missing rules, dead ends, or turns that are unclear before you commit them to paper.

text:
Integrated Marking Scheme
Your work is assessed out of 100 marks across seven criteria. For each, a mark band from 0–40%, 40–60%, 60–80%, and 80–100% describes the quality of your work, from unclear or missing evidence at the low end to polished, insightful, and highly effective work at the top.

Game Concept and Originality (15 marks): ranges from a concept that is unclear, generic, or heavily derivative, up to a concept that is highly inventive, distinctive, and immediately engaging.
Rules and Documentation Quality (15 marks): ranges from rules that are missing, unclear, or incomplete, up to rules that are precise, comprehensive, and can guide new players independently.
Board, Components, and Prototype Functionality (20 marks): ranges from a prototype that is missing or non-functional, up to a polished, coherent prototype with well-integrated components and strong usability.
Playtesting and Feedback Collection (15 marks): ranges from little or no meaningful playtest evidence, up to a thorough, well-run playtest with strong observations and high-quality feedback data.
Refinement and Iterative Improvement (15 marks): ranges from little change, or changes unrelated to feedback, up to targeted, well-justified refinements that clearly improve gameplay and show iterative thinking.
Reflection, Blog, and Process Evidence (10 marks): ranges from reflection that is missing or superficial with little process evidence, up to insightful, honest reflection with strong evidence of development across the project.
Presentation and Communication (10 marks): ranges from a presentation that is missing, unclear, or poorly structured, up to an engaging, polished presentation that communicates the full design journey effectively.

Notes on assessment:

Strong projects will show clear links between concept, prototype, playtest evidence, and final refinements.
Marks are awarded for process as well as final product.
Authentic evidence of development is essential.

You’re Starting in a Better Position Than You Think

title: Your Back-Safe Gym Plan
text:
The Three-Phase Plan
The programme is progressive, safe, and structured for the long game, moving through three phases: Foundation, Building, and Maintenance & Progression.

Phase 1: Foundation Phase
Weeks 1–4 · 3 sessions/week · Focus: Movement quality & core
Goal: Master safe movement patterns, wake up dormant muscles, and build a base without touching your back. Every set is about form — leave your ego at the door.
Monday · Session A — Lower Body + Core

Warm-up walk (back safe) — 10 min on treadmill, easy pace. Gets blood moving, loosens hips.
Glute Bridge (back safe) — 3 sets × 15 reps, bodyweight. Builds glutes that support your spine.
Leg Press (Machine) (back safe) — 3 sets × 12 reps, light weight. Safe alternative to squats — no spinal compression.
Dead Bug (back safe) — 3 sets × 10 reps each side. Your pilates background will help here — brilliant for deep core.
Bird Dog (back safe) — 3 sets × 10 reps each side. Trains spinal stabilisers — one of the best back-protection exercises.
Lying Hip Abduction (back safe) — 2 sets × 15 reps. Strengthens hip stabilisers that protect the lower back.

Wednesday · Session B — Cardio + Mobility

Stationary Bike or Rowing Machine (back safe) — 20–25 min, easy/moderate pace. Zone 2 cardio, brilliant for cholesterol and heart health. Bike is easiest on back; rowing builds back & core too but only once pain-free.
Hip Flexor Stretch (back safe) — 2 × 45 sec each side. Tight hip flexors are a major contributor to back pain.
Cat-Cow + Thoracic Rotation (back safe) — 2 × 10 reps. Keeps your spine mobile — you’ll know these from pilates.
Standing Calf Raises (back safe) — 3 × 20 reps. Zero spinal load, good for circulation.

Friday · Session C — Upper Body + Core

Lat Pulldown (Machine) (back safe) — 3 × 12 reps, light-moderate weight. Builds the lats that stabilise and protect your spine.
Seated Cable Row (back safe) — 3 × 12 reps. Keep your back upright and still — great upper back builder.
Chest Press (Machine) (back safe) — 3 × 12 reps. Machine keeps you stable — better than bench press while your back is building.
Plank (back safe) — 3 × 20–30 sec. Keep hips level. Build slowly. Stop if back twinges.
Pallof Press (Cable) (back safe) — 2 × 10 reps each side. Anti-rotation core exercise — protects the spine brilliantly.



Phase 2: Building Phase
Weeks 5–16 · 3–4 sessions/week · Focus: Muscle & Fitness
Goal: Progressive overload — gradually increase weight every 1–2 weeks. Introduce compound movements with care. Your core and glutes are now strong enough to protect you during bigger lifts.
Monday · Push Day — Chest · Shoulders · Triceps

Incline Dumbbell Press — 4 × 10–12. Easier on shoulders than flat bench, less lower-back arch needed.
Cable Lateral Raises — 3 × 15. Builds shoulder width, very low back stress.
Seated Shoulder Press (Machine) — 3 × 12. Machine keeps your back supported — avoid heavy barbell overhead pressing.
Tricep Pushdown (Cable) — 3 × 15. Great arm builder, zero back stress.
Plank Progressions (back safe) — 3 × 40–60 sec. Add side planks and plank reaches as you progress.

Tuesday · Cardio — Heart Health · Cholesterol

Zone 2 Cardio (back safe) — 30–40 min. Bike, cross-trainer or brisk walk. Zone 2 = you can hold a conversation. This is the single most effective thing for lowering LDL cholesterol and improving cardiovascular health.

Thursday · Pull Day — Back · Biceps · Rear Delts

Lat Pulldown — 4 × 10–12. Increase weight from Phase 1, wide grip for back width.
Seated Cable Row — 4 × 10–12. Focus on squeezing shoulder blades — builds the muscular corset around your spine.
Face Pulls (Cable) (back safe) — 3 × 15. One of the best exercises for posture and rotator cuff health — do these every session if you can.
Dumbbell Bicep Curls — 3 × 12. Seated to eliminate momentum and back strain.
Romanian Deadlift (Light) — 3 × 10. Dumbbell version, very light. Hip hinge movement — essential for back health when done correctly. Ask a trainer to check your form first.

Saturday · Leg Day — Glutes · Quads · Hamstrings

Hip Thrust (Barbell) (back safe) — 4 × 12. The king of glute exercises — zero spinal compression, massive benefit for back support.
Leg Press (back safe) — 4 × 12. Increase weight progressively. Keep lower back flat against pad at all times.
Leg Curl (Machine) — 3 × 12. Hamstrings support knee and hip — important for overall leg balance.
Goblet Squat (Dumbbell) — 3 × 12. Light weight, controlled. Safer than barbell squat — upright torso takes load off the spine.
Calf Raises + Core Finisher — 3 × 20 calves. Dead bugs + bird dogs to finish. Always end leg day with core work.



Phase 3: Maintenance & Progression Phase
Week 17 onwards · For life · Keep what you’ve built
Goal: This is the phase most people never reach — and the most important one. Keep 3–4 sessions per week, continue gradually increasing weight, and introduce variation to keep it enjoyable. At this point you can consider adding barbell squats or conventional deadlifts if your back feels consistently good — with a trainer present.
Progression rules:

Add 2.5–5kg when you can do all reps comfortably
Every 8 weeks, take a deload week (reduce weight 30%)
Try a new class or activity every 3 months
Keep pilates — it’s what keeps your back safe
Track your lifts (even a notebook counts)

Activities to add:

Swimming — incredible for the back and fitness
Cycling (indoor or outdoor)
Walking with poles (Nordic walking)
Yoga or mobility classes
Golf, tennis — once back is robust

title: Your Back-Safe Gym Plan
text:
Lowering Cholesterol
Exercise plus small diet tweaks make a powerful combination.

Zone 2 Cardio — 30–45 min, 2–3×/week at conversational pace. The most evidenced exercise for reducing LDL (“bad”) cholesterol and raising HDL (“good”) cholesterol.
Oily Fish — Salmon, mackerel, sardines 2–3×/week. Omega-3s directly lower triglycerides and raise HDL. One of the most impactful single food changes.
Oats Daily — Porridge or overnight oats for breakfast. Beta-glucan soluble fibre binds cholesterol in the gut, clinically proven to reduce LDL by 5–10%.
Healthy Fats In — Avocado, olive oil, nuts (especially walnuts & almonds), seeds. Swap saturated fats from processed food for these.
Talk to Your GP — If your cholesterol is high, your doctor may want to run a blood panel after 3 months of exercise and diet changes. Some people also benefit from plant sterols/stanols.
Muscle Helps — Building muscle mass improves insulin sensitivity and lipid metabolism. The strength training in this plan directly contributes to better cholesterol over time.

title: Your Back-Safe Gym Plan
text:
What to Expect & When

Week 2 — You’ll feel the difference. Better energy, sleeping better, muscles feel more “switched on”. Some DOMS (muscle soreness) is normal — pain in the back or joints is a signal to stop and reassess.
Week 4 — Neural gains kick in. Your lifts will increase quickly at first — this is your nervous system learning, not just muscle growth. This phase feels great. Don’t let it tempt you to go too heavy too fast.
Week 8 — Visible changes begin. Clothes fit differently, posture is noticeably better. Core strength is improving measurably. Back should feel more supported day-to-day.
Week 12 — First blood test check-in. Good time to get cholesterol checked if you started high. Muscle mass building seriously underway. Fitness levels noticeably improved.
6 Months — The big shift. Significant muscle gain, much stronger core, back pain episodes should be noticeably less frequent and less severe. The gym is now a habit, not a chore.

title: Your Back-Safe Gym Plan
text:
Making It Enjoyable & Sustainable
The best plan is the one you actually stick to.

Build a Playlist — A dedicated gym playlist that you only listen to in the gym trains your brain to associate it with getting motivated. Your reward system works for you.
Track Your Lifts — Nothing is more motivating than seeing the numbers go up. A simple notebook or free app (Strong, FitNotes) means you always know what to beat.
Find a Training Buddy — Even once a week with a friend dramatically increases adherence. Also makes the session fly by and means someone can keep an eye on your form.
Schedule It Like a Meeting — Put your three sessions in the calendar. Treat them as non-negotiable appointments. Miss one? Don’t compensate — just show up for the next one.
Small Wins First — In week 1, your goal is simply: show up. Add one more push-up, one more kg. Celebrate the process, not just the end goal.
Variety Every 8 Weeks — Swap exercises for variations — swap leg press for goblet squat, swap lat pulldown grip width. Fresh enough to stay engaged, consistent enough to progress.

title: Your Back-Safe Gym Plan
text:
Back Protection Rules — Non-Negotiable
Before every session:

5–10 min warm-up always — never skip
Cat-cow and hip circles before leg/core work
Start lighter than you think you need to

Pain protocol:

Soreness in muscles = fine, expected
Any sharp or shooting back pain = stop immediately
Dull back ache during exercise = reduce weight, check form
Check in: how does your back feel today?
Pain that lasts more than 48hrs = see your physio
Check yourself in gym mirrors — they’re there to help

Posture cues:

Neutral spine always — not arched, not rounded
Brace your core before every lift (gentle tension)
Hinge at hips, not the waist, for any bending

Recovery:

7–8 hours sleep — when muscles (and backs) repair
Protein within an hour of training
Stretch hips and hamstrings on rest days
Keep your pilates session — it’s part of the plan

title: Your Back-Safe Gym Plan
text:
Summary
This back-safe gym plan takes you through three progressive phases — Foundation, Building, and Maintenance — moving from careful movement quality work towards fuller strength training, while always protecting your spine. Alongside training, small diet changes (Zone 2 cardio, oily fish, oats, healthy fats) support lower cholesterol, and simple habits like tracking lifts, scheduling sessions, and finding a training buddy will help the plan stick for the long term.
Above all, follow the non-negotiable back protection rules: always warm up, watch for pain signals, keep a neutral spine, and prioritise recovery. This plan is general fitness guidance, not medical advice. Always consult your GP and physiotherapist before starting, especially given your back injury history, and listen to your body above all else.
